01 · Instrument Overview

What you're supporting

The GASTAT‑700 series is Techno Medica's point‑of‑care blood gas / electrolyte / metabolite analyzer line. Eight product codes cover four hardware tiers (710, 720, 730, 735), each available with or without the Auto QC (aqc) option — same chassis, same reagent system, different electrode complement.

Product line-up (operation manual, System Description)

Model number and Auto QC status print on every result and appear top‑right of the touch screen — check it before quoting a spec range to a user; the 730/735 add Glc/Lac and CO‑OXY parameters the 710/720 don't measure. See Model Comparison.

Why end users like it

Straight from the manual's own feature list — useful vocabulary when you're explaining the value proposition to a lab director or ICU head nurse:

  • One‑touch operation — mount the sample container, press Analysis
  • Liquid calibration system — no compressed gas cylinder to manage
  • Micro mode down to 40 µL for pediatric / difficult draws
  • Absolute hands‑free sampling — minimizes biohazard exposure
  • Long shelf‑life Glc/Lac electrodes; zero routine electrode maintenance
  • Automatic de‑proteinizing clean built into the CAL Cartridge cycle
  • IoT maintenance booking, electrode condition & reagent status on the home screen
  • 12.1″ colour touch panel; built‑in battery for power‑failure protection

Thirteen positions in a single removable cartridge bay — knowing this layout by number is the fastest way to talk a user through "which electrode is Cl" over the phone.

02 · Measurement Principles

Two electrode families, one sample path

Every electrode in the module is either amperometric (measures a current produced by a reaction — pO₂) or potentiometric (measures a voltage difference against a reference — pH, pCO₂, Na, K, Cl, iCa). Knowing which family an electrode belongs to is what makes a calibration‑failure conversation with service make sense.

This section works through the electrochemistry parameter‑by‑parameter — the level of detail worth having on hand when a user asks "why does this need a membrane at all" or a service call gets into which electrode is actually at fault.

pO₂ — amperometric, Clark-type electrode

pCO₂ — potentiometric, Severinghaus electrode

Not a direct CO₂ sensor: it's a pH electrode wrapped around a bicarbonate buffer, reading the pH shift that dissolved CO₂ causes.

pH — potentiometric, glass membrane electrode

The same potentiometric principle as the ISE electrodes below, using a pH‑sensitive glass membrane instead of an ion‑selective one: the membrane develops a voltage proportional to the difference in H⁺ activity between the sample and an internal reference solution, read against the external Reference electrode. The underlying physics is the Nernst equation — see the equation box under Parameters & Equations.

Na⁺ / K⁺ / Cl⁻ / iCa²⁺ — potentiometric, ion-selective electrodes (ISE) & Reference

This is the practical reason the manual splits calibration‑failure troubleshooting into pH/Na/K/Cl/Ca vs Reference vs pCO₂/pO₂ vs Glc/Lac groups (see Troubleshooting) — each group fails for different physical reasons.

Glc & Lac — amperometric enzyme electrodes

A third electrode family: neither a bare metal amperometric sensor nor a bare ISE, but an enzyme layer bonded onto the platinum surface that turns an otherwise electro‑inactive analyte into one that is.

Glc electrode — glucose oxidase (GOD) membrane, +0.65 V applied
StepReaction
Enzyme layerD‑Glucose + O₂ + H₂O →GOD D‑Gluconic acid + H₂O₂
Cathode (Pt)O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O
AnodeH₂O₂ → 2H⁺ + O₂ + 2e⁻
Lac electrode — lactate oxidase (LOD) membrane
StepReaction
Enzyme layerL‑Lactate + O₂ →LOD Pyruvate + H₂O₂
Cathode (Pt)O₂ + 4H⁺ + 4e⁻ → 2H₂O
AnodeH₂O₂ → 2H⁺ + O₂ + 2e⁻

Both electrodes ultimately measure the same thing electrochemically — the H₂O₂ produced by the enzyme reaction, oxidised at the platinum surface — which is why both sit in the calibration‑failure troubleshooting group together (Troubleshooting) and why a discoloured or exhausted enzyme membrane, not just a dirty electrode, is the first thing worth suspecting when only these two go bad.

Hb, CO-oximetry & bilirubin — multi-wavelength spectrophotometry

A completely different measurement family from the two above: no electrode at all. The optional CO‑OXY / Hb module (730/735 tier) haemolyses a small aliquot and passes it through a flow cell that's read at multiple infrared/visible wavelengths, then resolves the individual haemoglobin fractions and bilirubin by multivariate analysis of the absorbance spectrum.

ParameterPrinciple
cHbTwo‑wavelength infrared absorbance — totals only Oxy‑Hb and Deoxy‑Hb; ignores MetHb/COHb, so it under‑reports total Hb whenever those fractions are elevated
ctHbFull multi‑wavelength co‑oximetry — resolves all four fractions (O₂Hb, HHb, COHb, MetHb) by multivariate analysis, so it correctly accounts for MetHb/COHb in the total
sO₂, FO₂Hb, FHHb, FCOHb, FMetHbEach fraction resolved from the same multi‑wavelength absorbance spectrum as ctHb
ctBilMultivariate analysis of the same absorbance spectrum at bilirubin‑sensitive wavelengths
cHb vs ctHb isn't a rounding difference. A smoker or a CO‑poisoning patient with real carboxyhaemoglobin will read a falsely‑low total hemoglobin on cHb because that measurement simply doesn't see COHb. If the site's protocol calls for CO‑OXY fractions, make sure the total Hb being charted is ctHb, not cHb.

Two-point calibration

Every measurement is anchored between two calibrator levels from the CAL Cartridge. The instrument reads the electrode's signal at Cal 1 and Cal 2, draws the line between them, and interpolates the sample's concentration from where its signal falls on that line.

Automatic calibration schedule — symbols shown on the Calibration → Calibration schedule grid
SymbolActionWhat runs
○1‑point calibrationCAL 1 liquid only
◎2‑point calibrationCAL 1 + CAL 2 liquid
CInternal cleaner + 2‑pointInternal cleaner runs first, then a full 2‑point calibration — must appear at least once per day; takes ≈15 min
(blank)No calibration—
If 1‑point calibration hasn't run in 2 hours, or 2‑point in 5 hours, the instrument blocks analysis and asks for calibration before it will accept a sample.

Correction factor & site verification

Reached at Function → Others → Self diagnostic → Correction factor — a slope and offset (intercept) applied per parameter, per sample type, on top of the normal calibration curve.

Shipped factory‑optimised. The manual is blunt about this one: don't touch it unless a Techno Medica representative has authorised the change — an incorrect correction factor produces confidently wrong results, not an error message. Deactivated parameters can't have a correction factor entered; three independent sets exist for the three dialysate modes. A related screen, CRS correction factor, will calculate the Na/K/Cl correction automatically from an ISE‑CRS run against its certified value — that's the sanctioned way to nudge these three back into line.

How each one is actually derived

Techno Medica doesn't publish its internal regression constants in the manuals on hand — what follows is the standard Henderson‑Hasselbalch / Siggaard‑Andersen framework that blood‑gas analyzers implement industry‑wide, which is what these symbols are actually computing under the hood. Useful for sanity‑checking a strange result by hand, or for explaining to a resident why two numbers on the slip must move together.

Acid–base & buffers

ParameterEquation
cHCO3⁻‑act0.0307 × pCO₂ × 10(pH − 6.105)
ctCO2(P)cHCO3⁻‑act + (0.0307 × pCO₂)  — adds back the dissolved‑CO₂ term
cBE(B)  (blood)(1 − 0.014×ctHb) × [(cHCO3⁻‑act − 24.4) + (9.5+1.63×ctHb)×(pH − 7.40)]
cBE(ecf)  (standard)same Van Slyke form with ctHb fixed at 5 g/dL ≈ cHCO3⁻‑act − 24.8 + 16.2×(pH − 7.40)
cHCO3⁻‑stdRead from the Siggaard‑Andersen alignment nomogram at pCO₂ = 40 Torr, fully O₂‑saturated blood, 37 °C — no closed‑form equation, derived alongside BE(ecf)
AGcNa⁺ − (cCl⁻ + cHCO3⁻‑act)
AG(K)(cNa⁺ + cK⁺) − (cCl⁻ + cHCO3⁻‑act)
cCa²⁺(7.4)cCa²⁺ × [1 − 0.53 × (7.40 − pH)]  — corrects ionised calcium for the pH‑dependence of albumin binding; exact coefficient is vendor‑calibrated

05 · Sample & Operation Workflow

From draw to printed result

Sample requirements

  • Collect only when the patient is in a stable steady state
  • Use a syringe heparinized with lithium or balanced heparin — Techno Medica recommends a dedicated blood‑gas syringe
  • Remove all air bubbles before mixing — trapped air falsely raises pO₂
  • Mix thoroughly with the anticoagulant to ensure homogeneity
  • Roll the syringe 20–30 times between both palms immediately before analysis, then eject a couple of drops to tissue to clear the tip of air
If the sample can't be run immediately
ContainerStorageTime limit
Plastic syringeRoom temperature≤ 15 min
Glass syringeRefrigerator or iced water≤ 30 min

Container & Micro Mode selection

ContainerMicro modeUse it when
SyringeOFFStandard syringe sample, 195 µL
SyringeONSmall syringe volume — 40 µL
CapillaryOFFStandard capillary tube, 80–100 µL (model dependent)
CapillaryONSmall capillary volume — 40 µL

Running a syringe sample

  1. Confirm Ready
    Instrument status shows Ready and the sample type icon shows blood. If it shows "△ Ready for some parameters" or "× Not Ready", clear that first.
  2. Mix
    Roll the syringe 20–30 times between both palms, then invert until thoroughly mixed.
  3. Scan (optional)
    Scan the syringe barcode to attach a sample ID.
  4. Load & press Analysis
    Seat the syringe on the Sample Port and press Analysis. Confirm the button is actually activated before walking away.
  5. Aspiration & measurement
    The screen switches automatically; the instrument aspirates the sample and begins analysis unattended.
  6. Remove the syringe
    Remove after the on‑screen prompt — the instrument beeps if you don't remove it.
  7. Check for a micro‑mode prompt
    If sample volume was too small or air bubbles were detected, the display recommends re‑running under Micro mode.
  8. Enter patient info & review
    Add patient details if required. Result reports to display and printer; a Flush sequence starts automatically afterward.

Running a capillary sample

  1. Confirm Ready
    Status is Ready and sample type icon shows blood.
  2. Mix with the magnet
    Move the capillary's internal mixing magnet back and forth along the tube, 20 passes each direction.
  3. Scan (optional)
    Scan the capillary barcode for sample ID.
  4. Load firmly & press Analysis
    Seat the capillary firmly on the Sample Port, confirm Analysis is activated.
  5. Aspiration & measurement
    Automatic, as with syringe mode.
  6. Remove after the prompt; enter patient info
    Same beep‑on‑non‑removal behaviour and micro‑mode advisory as the syringe path.
Micro mode (40 µL): don't forget to mix the sample and expel 2–3 drops from the syringe tip before loading. The instrument will prompt with an OK message before it accepts a micro sample.

06 · Interferences

What can throw a result off

Techno Medica doesn't publish a dedicated, package‑insert‑style interference table for the GASTAT‑700 series — there's no chapter listing icterus, lipemia or specific drugs against each parameter (searched the full operation and service manuals for "interference" — zero hits). What the manuals do contain is a set of real, scattered interference and pre‑analytical‑error notes, spread across the sample‑handling tips and the Q&A troubleshooting table. Consolidated by parameter below.

Documented in the Techno Medica manuals
Parameter(s)Interferent / conditionEffectSource
Na, K, iCaAnticoagulant other than Lithium/sodium heparin used in the syringeResult skewed away from the true electrolyte valueManual
KHemolyzed sampleFalsely elevated — intracellular K released into plasmaManual
pO₂Air bubble not removed before mixing the sampleFalsely increased — sample equilibrates toward room‑air pO₂Manual
Glc, LacDelay between draw and measurementGlc falsely low, Lac falsely high — ongoing in‑vitro glycolysisManual
Hb / tHb / CO‑OXY fractionsFlow cell data sheet not scanned, or Flow cell installed incorrectly; sample not mixed wellDisagrees with a hematology‑analyzer comparatorManual
Any parameterClot, unremoved air bubble, wrong storage time/temperature, or over‑dilution by anticoagulantResult “remarkably high or low”Manual
Flow path (indirect — Hb/CO‑OXY optics)Hyperlipidaemic sampleClogs the flow path — needs an External Cleaning cycle (≈19 min) before results can be trusted againManual

Sources: Analyzing Samples & sample‑handling tips, Q&A / System trouble table, and the Cleaning Function chapter of the operation manual.

Not in the Techno Medica manuals — standard clinical‑chemistry knowledge for these measurement principles, added for context rather than sourced from the manual: multi‑wavelength CO‑oximetry (Hb fractions, bilirubin) is optically sensitive to icteric and lipemic samples across brands — inspect visually before running, and cross‑check against a hematology analyzer if the sample looks abnormal. Ionized calcium (iCa) is pH‑dependent — a warmed or delayed sample can shift iCa even with the correct anticoagulant, for the same underlying reason pH itself drifts. Treat these as general caveats to apply judgement with, not GASTAT‑confirmed behaviour.
07 · Reagents & Calibration

The CAL Cartridge system

No gas cylinder: one CAL Cartridge carries both calibration levels plus the cleaning liquid, and the instrument calibrates itself against it on a schedule you configure.

#ItemVolumeIngredients
1Calibration solution 1300 mLBuffer agent, surfactant, antiseptic agent, detergent, salts, glucose, lactate, deionised water, gases
2Calibration solution 2200 mLSame base formulation as solution 1, second calibration point
3Cleaning liquid80 mLDetergent, antiseptic agent, salts, deionised water
Shelf life: 9 months from manufacture, 1 month once on‑board (regardless of sample volume). Store 4–25 °C. Can be removed and re‑seated once — a second removal forces a fresh barcode scan.
Save mode stretches on‑board life to 2 months — but it cannot be used on AQC models with Glc/Lac enabled.

Flush & Waste

ConsumableRoleNotes
Flush solutionFlow‑path cleaning after every calibration and every 20 minutes of conditioning9‑month shelf life from manufacture; used until it expires regardless of throughput; store 4–25 °C
Waste bottleCollects spent flush solutionThe empty Flush bottle itself becomes the Waste bottle once re‑labelled — the instrument alerts at 90% full
CleanerRuns every 50 analyses, or on a fixed scheduleAlso runs as part of daily “C” calibration cycle

Replacing the CAL Cartridge

  1. Warm to room temperature
    Take the cartridge out of the fridge ≥ 6 hours ahead, until the reagent is no longer cold.
  2. Mix
    Rotate flat/horizontally for 1–2 minutes to fully re‑homogenise the solution.
  3. Remove the old pack
    The Replacement screen appears automatically.
  4. Scan & load
    Scan barcode 1 (CAL Cartridge) then barcode 2 (AQC data), then load the new cartridge per the on‑screen / video prompt. The instrument auto‑calibrates — wait for Ready.
The instrument reboots its application once daily at a fixed time to run the internal cleaner — it won't reboot mid‑security‑entry, mid‑self‑diagnostic, mid‑consumable screen, or with a sample loaded. It will, however, reboot on its own if the measurement module cover opens, a reagent bottle is pulled, or a Flow/Temperature/consumable error fires — worth knowing before you assume a spontaneous restart is a fault.
08 · Quality Control

Four QC layers

LayerWhat it checks
GASTROL‑QCAmpouled external control material at defined levels — the traditional cross‑check against a certified target
ISE CRSCertified reference solution for the ion‑selective electrodes specifically
Dialysate controlControl material matched to dialysate sample analysis
AQC (Auto QC)Instrument‑internal control run automatically on a schedule — the day‑to‑day safety net between GASTROL runs

GASTROL‑QC — getting a clean run

Most "bad GASTROL result" calls trace back to ampoule handling, not the instrument:

  • Shake the ampoule vigorously for ≥ 15 seconds immediately before use to re‑equilibrate gases
  • Single‑use only — use the exclusive adapter
  • Measure immediately after opening — room air shifts pH, pCO₂ and pO₂ fast
  • If storage wasn't 22–28 °C, equilibrate ≥ 60 min at 22–28 °C (or ≥ 10 min at 25 °C in a constant‑temperature bath) before use
  • Check the expiry date and watch for air bubbles in the ampoule
  • Confirm the target value is correctly entered in the QC menu

If it's still out of range: check Electrode condition for a failed calibration and fix that first, then try replacing the CAL Cartridge and re‑running a 2‑point calibration, then the specific electrode. Allow ≈30 minutes for a freshly replaced electrode to stabilise, and repeat 2‑point calibration manually until it passes.

09 · Result Interpretation

Reading the printed slip

Every value on a GASTAT printout can carry a flag character. Knowing the legend by heart is what lets you tell a nurse over the phone whether a result is trustworthy in fifteen seconds.

Flag legend
FlagMeaning
noneWithin normal range
+++Above the electrode's upper measurement range
−−−Below the electrode's lower measurement range
HAbove the normal range, within measurement range
LBelow the normal range, within measurement range
*Air bubble detected, or sample volume too small
?Instrument could not analyse the sample
cLatest calibration failed — check Electrode condition
aLatest AQC was out of range — check Electrode condition
A calculated parameter prints as **.* / ***.* when one of its measured inputs is itself unreadable — e.g. Base Excess can't be derived without a valid pH and pCO₂. Don't treat a stray asterisk field as a separate fault; trace it back to the flagged measured parameter first.

Worked example

The printout above, annotated — a genuinely critical gas that's worth being able to read at a glance:

[ GASTAT‑1820 Analysis result ]
Sample type : Blood sample

pH     7.188  L  ← below 7.380–7.460, acidaemic
pCO2   10.0 Torr  ——— ← below the 10.0 measurement floor
pO2    210.0 Torr H  ← well above 74–108 (patient on high FiO₂, 21.0% shown — check the source)
Na     155.2 mmol/L H
K      1.00 mmol/L  ——— ← below the 1.00 measurement floor, critical
Cl     139.8 mmol/L H
Ca     0.50 mmol/L  ——— ← below the 0.50 measurement floor
Hb     8.8 g/dL   L

AG     11.7 mmol/L  within range despite the chaos above
HCO3‑act 3.7 mmol/L  ← severely low — consistent with the low pH
BE(ecf) ***.*    ← uncalculable, inputs out of range

Reading it in one pass: acidaemic (pH 7.19) with a very low bicarbonate and multiple electrolytes pegged at the instrument's measurement floor or ceiling — this slip is a strong prompt to double‑check sample integrity (clot, dilution, wrong tube) before it's reported as a patient result, not just a QC problem.

Orienting an acid–base result

A systematic read, step by step

  1. pH — acidaemic or alkalaemic?
    <7.35 is acidaemia, >7.45 is alkalaemia. A normal pH doesn't rule out a disorder — it can mean none is present, or two opposing ones are fully compensating each other.
  2. Which primary process explains the pH?
    pCO₂ moving with pH (both up or both down) is metabolic; pCO₂ moving opposite pH is respiratory. Confirm against cHCO3⁻‑act moving the same direction as the metabolic call.
  3. Is the compensation appropriate?
    Use the expected‑value formulas below. A measured pCO₂/HCO3⁻ that lands outside the expected window means a second, independent disorder is present — not just an unusually large compensation.
  4. Calculate the anion gap
    If elevated, work the MUDPILES / normal‑AG tables below. If albumin is low, correct the gap first (each 1 g/dL drop in albumin below 4 g/dL hides ≈2.5 mmol/L of gap).
  5. Elevated AG? Check the delta ratio
    Delta ratio = ΔAG ÷ ΔHCO3⁻ = (AG − 12) ÷ (24 − HCO3⁻‑act). ≈1–2 is a pure high‑AG metabolic acidosis; <1 suggests a concurrent normal‑AG acidosis; >2 suggests a concurrent metabolic alkalosis (or a pre‑existing high HCO3⁻) is masking part of the acidosis.
  6. Layer in oxygenation
    A-a gradient and P/F ratio (below) tell you whether the lungs themselves are the problem, independent of the acid‑base call.

Expected compensation

If the measured pCO₂ or HCO3⁻ falls outside the window these formulas predict, stop treating it as compensation — there are two primary disorders, not one.

Primary disorderExpected compensation
Metabolic acidosisexpected pCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO3⁻) + 8 ± 2  (Winter's formula)
Metabolic alkalosisexpected pCO₂ = (0.7 × HCO3⁻) + 20 ± 5
Respiratory acidosis, acuteHCO3⁻ rises ≈1 mmol/L per 10 Torr pCO₂ rise
Respiratory acidosis, chronicHCO3⁻ rises ≈3.5–4 mmol/L per 10 Torr pCO₂ rise
Respiratory alkalosis, acuteHCO3⁻ falls ≈2 mmol/L per 10 Torr pCO₂ fall
Respiratory alkalosis, chronicHCO3⁻ falls ≈4–5 mmol/L per 10 Torr pCO₂ fall

Anion gap — working the differential

High AG (>16 mmol/L) — MUDPILES
MMethanol
UUraemia
DDiabetic ketoacidosis
PParaldehyde / Propylene glycol
IIron / Isoniazid
LLactic acidosis
EEthylene glycol
SSalicylates
Normal AG (hyperchloraemic)
GI bicarbonate lossDiarrhoea, ileostomy, fistula
Renal tubular acidosisType 1, 2 or 4 RTA
Early renal failureBefore uraemic acids accumulate
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitorsAcetazolamide
Post‑hypocapniaRapid correction of respiratory alkalosis
DilutionalLarge‑volume saline resuscitation

Oxygenation: P/F ratio & A–a gradient

pO2/FiO₂ (P/F) ratio — ARDS severity, Berlin definition (with PEEP ≥ 5 cmH₂O)
P/F ratioCategory
> 300No ARDS by this criterion
200–300Mild
100–200Moderate
< 100Severe

Expected A–a gradient rises with age (rough rule of thumb: age ÷ 4 + 4 Torr on room air). A widened gradient with hypoxaemia points to V/Q mismatch, shunt, or a diffusion defect — a normal gradient with hypoxaemia points instead to hypoventilation or a low inspired O₂ (altitude, FiO₂ error), since the lungs themselves are transferring oxygen normally.

A second worked example — compensated, not simple

A patient with known COPD, sample: pH 7.34, pCO₂ 68 Torr, cHCO3⁻‑act 36 mmol/L.

pH is low‑normal‑ish but still acidaemic, pCO₂ is markedly high → primary respiratory acidosis. HCO3⁻ has risen from a baseline of ≈24 to 36, i.e. +12 for a pCO₂ rise of +28 over the normal 40 — that's ≈4.3 mmol/L of HCO3⁻ per 10 Torr of pCO₂, squarely in the chronic compensation range (3.5–4/10 Torr) rather than the acute one (1/10 Torr). Reads as a chronic, compensated respiratory acidosis consistent with the patient's COPD — not a fresh acute event. If the same numbers showed HCO3⁻ still near 24, that mismatch would flag an acute decompensation superimposed on top.

10 · Maintenance & Self-Diagnostic

Cleaning & the built-in diagnostic suite

Cleaning typeWhen
FlushEvery cycle, after every calibration; also every 20 minutes as background conditioning
Cleaner (built into CAL Cartridge)Every 50 sample analyses, or on the daily “C” schedule slot (see Reagents & Calibration)
Internal cleaningOn demand for suspected clogging or carry‑over — takes ≈10 minutes; run a 2‑point calibration immediately after
External cleaningSample port / sampling nozzle clogged or stained
Hb cleaningFlow cell (CO‑OXY / Hb module) clogged or stained

Self-diagnostic

Two numbers worth memorising from the Flow‑cell light‑intensity self‑diagnostic (used when troubleshooting Hb/CO‑OXY calibration failures — see Troubleshooting): above 63000 usually means the Flow cell isn't seated correctly; below 20000 usually means it's dirty.

11 · Troubleshooting

Getting back to Ready

The standby screen carries three independent status fields — Instrument, Maintenance, and Electrode — and they fail independently. Read all three before you start swapping parts.

Error codes

CodeErrorProbable causeFix
03600Temperature errorCold start, just after power‑on or electrode replacement; module cover open; room >30 °C or fan obstructedClose the module cover, wait 3–30 min depending on cause, run Self‑diagnostic (temperature); confirm room is 10–30 °C with clear airflow to the fan
—Flow sensor errorLiquid not detected at the flow sensor — tubing dislodged, dirty, pinched, or the sensor cover isn't seatedRun Self‑diagnostic (Flow); check tubing routing, sample port/nozzle seating and clots, O‑ring and electrode seating
—Measurement module cover openCover not fully closed, often because an electrode isn't seatedCheck electrode seating, then close the cover until it clicks
03744Flow cell installation errorFlow cell not seated firmlyRe‑insert until it clicks
03703Waste bottle errorWaste bottle fullReplace the Waste bottle
03731Flush bottle emptyFlush solution can't feed, or is insufficientReplace the Flush bottle
—CAL Cartridge emptyCalibration liquid can't feed, or is insufficientReplace the CAL Cartridge
03803Battery errorRunning on battery and it's insufficient — display stops respondingBattery switch OFF → power switch OFF → connect AC → power ON → battery switch ON
03802No calibration conducted>2h since last 1‑point, or >5h since last 2‑point, or none since power‑onRun the indicated calibration before analysis

Calibration failure — corrective action by electrode group

The manual splits this by which electrodes share a physical failure mode — work down the list for the affected group before reaching for a replacement part.

pH / Na / K / Cl / Ca (fix Reference first if 2+ parameters fail together)
  1. Shake the electrode to clear air from its sample path
  2. Check solution level; if low, discard (avoid concentration drift) and refill
  3. Check for leaks; wipe dry if needed
  4. Check the electrode's O‑ring and its holder's O‑ring are seated
  5. Check the sample path for clots; remove neighbouring electrodes to clean if needed
  6. Confirm calibration solution actually reaches the measurement unit — check for air bubbles, pump tube, tubing, port, nozzle
  7. Replace the electrode if unresolved; replace the CAL Cartridge if solution won't aspirate
Reference electrode
  1. Shake so Ref solution reaches the sample path
  2. Check solution level; refill if low
  3. Check for leaks; wipe dry
  4. Check O‑ring seating
  5. Check for KCl crystal at the sample path — wash with distilled water, refill
  6. Check the sample path for clots
  7. Confirm calibration solution reaches the unit without air bubbles
  8. Replace the electrode if unresolved
pCO₂ / pO₂
  1. Shake to clear air from the sample path
  2. Check solution reaches the inner electrode; if the inner solution is empty or discoloured, replace
  3. Check O‑ring seating
  4. Check the sample path for clots
  5. Confirm calibration solution reaches the unit without air bubbles
  6. Replace the electrode if unresolved
  7. Replace the CAL Cartridge if still unresolved
Glc / Lac
  1. Shake to clear air from the sample path
  2. Check solution reaches the inner electrode; replace if empty/discoloured
  3. Check O‑ring seating
  4. Check the sample path for clots
  5. Confirm calibration solution reaches the unit without air bubbles
  6. Check the Reference electrode's sample path for crystallisation or clot
  7. Replace the electrode if unresolved

Electrode voltage drops if the sample path dries out from prolonged idle time.

Hb / CO‑OXY
  1. Check the Flow cell is installed correctly
  2. Self‑diagnose (Electrode) and check light intensity: >63000 → reseat the Flow cell; <20000 → clean it (Flush + Internal cleaning), then re‑test
  3. If still abnormal, clean the Oxy line
  4. Replace the Flow cell if unresolved
All parameters failing together
  1. Run Flush cleaning and Internal cleaning
  2. Check every O‑ring is seated
  3. Check the sample path for clots
  4. Confirm calibration solution reaches the unit without air bubbles — check tube, port, nozzle

Barcode, printer & display

SymptomFix
No “Barcode Read OK” printedCheck thermal paper has enough margin
Barcode won't readConfirm the reader emits light; try the spare barcode on the consumable's box — the label may be defective
No printing at allPrinter door open; out of paper; paper loaded inside‑out; printed‑sheet counter at 0
Print faint / crooked / smearedClear obstructions around the print head and platen roller
Nothing on displayConfirm power is on and the cord is seated; check nothing is blocking the human‑detect sensor (display sleeps if no one is detected)
Display misaligned / dim / off‑colourRun touch panel calibration; adjust display settings

System Q&A

SymptomFix
No movement at allCheck the power cord and that the power switch is on
Sample won't aspirateCheck for a clot or air bubble in the syringe, and confirm the syringe actually contains anticoagulant
Dead after a nearby lightning strikeLikely a blown fuse — battery switch OFF, unplug (instrument end last), remove the fuse box, replace both fuses, reseat until it clicks, reconnect power (wall end first), battery switch ON
“Waste bottle is full” when it isn'tThe last replacement likely wasn't logged correctly — redo Waste bottle replacement through the proper menu flow
“Sample not detected” with sample loadedRun Flush cleaning; check the container for a clot and expel a couple of drops before loading
Sample‑result flags * (air/short sample), c (calibration failed) and a (AQC failed) are covered with the full flag legend in Result Interpretation — they're a patient‑result problem, not an instrument fault, and the fix is upstream (fix the calibration/AQC, then re‑run the sample).
12 · Model Comparison

710 → 735: what actually changes

All four tiers share the same chassis, reagent system and 12.1″ touch panel. What changes is the electrode/optics complement — confirmed here from the home‑screen parameter bars themselves, which is the fastest way to identify an unlabelled unit in the field.

GASTAT‑710 / 710aqc

  • Blood gas + electrolytes
  • pH, pCO₂, pO₂, Na, K, Cl, iCa
  • Entry tier of the line

GASTAT‑720 / 720aqc

  • Gas + electrolytes + Hb
  • Adds single‑parameter Hb
  • Capillary volume: 80 µL

GASTAT‑730 / 730aqc

  • Gas + electrolytes + metabolites
  • Adds Glc, Lac
  • Capillary volume: 100 µL

GASTAT‑735 / 735aqc

  • Full panel + CO‑oximetry
  • Adds Glc, Lac, tHb, sO₂, FO₂Hb, FCOHb, FMetHb, tBil
  • Widest home‑screen parameter bar of the line
The aqc suffix adds the Auto QC module on any tier — it doesn't change the measured‑parameter set. All sample volumes and shared specs (195 µL syringe, 40 µL micro mode, CAL Cartridge system, calibration workflow) are identical across the line — only capillary volume and the parameter set change between tiers. Always confirm the exact configuration against the product code on the unit's home screen (see Instrument Overview) before quoting a spec to a customer.
